newsitem.title: UK: Major, Blair vie for votes on the battle bus.
newsitem.headline: Major, Blair vie for votes on the battle bus.

text.p: John Major got a present from the journalists on his plane last week -- a T-shirt with the slogan "John and Norma's extended family."

The phrase was one which the British prime minister had used to describe the horde of cameramen and reporters who have chronicled his every step during a six-week election campaign now drawing to a close.

Major, criss-crossing Britain in a desperate mission to reverse disastrous poll ratings before the May 1 election, was delighted, calling his wife, Norma, to come back from the front of the plane to get one, too.
No journalist has yet tried to present his Labour rival, Tony Blair, with a T-shirt and there has been no suggestion that Blair considers the trailing media pack to be part of his family.
Instead, Blair is determined to transform the media from the traditional obstacle to a Labour government into the means to his desired end -- a Labour government after 18 years of Conservative rule.
Major may stroll to the back of the plane for a drink with the journalists, ruffling the hair of a BBC television presenter after an awkward question, but access to Blair is tightly controlled.

Major's decision to stage the longest election campaign in 80 years to try to cling on to power launched the two leaders on a marathon journey for votes covering several hundred, at times even a thousand or more, miles (kms) a day.

Both have made speeches and walkabouts in town centres a key part of their campaigns. But behind the traditional style is a ruthless use of modern technology and strategies largely tried and tested in the United States.

Labour in particular, with close links to U.S. President Bill Clinton's campaign strategists, has relied heavily on focus groups -- extensive discussions with small, selected groups -- to refine a message best suited to the electorate.
The opposition party's "war book" -- exhibited by the Conservatives last week in a media coup -- showed meticulous day-by-day planning in getting the message across.
Both parties are using high-powered advertising agencies to attack their opponents and to grab voters' attention, overshadowing the minority parties also contesting the election.

But the daily gossip from the campaign trail -- and the atmosphere on the so-called "battle buses" carrying the media behind the two leaders' private vehicles -- assumed growing importance as the duel became an ever more bitter and personal.
Major began the campaign with gusto, clearly enjoying the escape from the straitjacket of government and the constraints of keeping his fractious party together.
Despite Labour's initial poll lead of 20 points or more, he enthused party staff with his belief that the Conservatives, by casting themselves as the underdogs, could snatch a narrow victory.

But as polls continued to show a solid Labour lead, and party members began openly speculating about his successor as party leader, Major's good humour has given way at times to anger and frustration.
He was grim when photographers on tour with him turned up in another T-shirt bearing a Labour campaign slogan: "Things can only get better."

Blair, apart from a day or so of apparent uncertainty when polls seemed to show a dip and he stumbled in a couple of interviews, has appeared ever more focussed. Nothing was left to chance and even his impromptu moments were choreographed.

So far, apart from an allegation -- later admitted -- that a journalist took heroin on Major's plane, the campaign has lacked the kind of titillating antics that made "Primary Colors", about a U.S. election campaign bearing similarities to Clinton's run for the While House, into a best seller.
But whatever happens on Thursday -- a landslide victory for Labour or one of the most startling political upsets in British political history -- history has been made again on the campaign trail.
